title: The Cost of Sleep
summary: Akbar complains of insomnia on a bed of royal velvet, while an exhausted sentry sleeps soundly on cold stone. Birbal reveals the secret of sweet sleep.
full_text:
One morning, Emperor Akbar arrived at the council hall looking pale, weary, and irritable. He had tossed and turned all night upon his bed of swan feathers and embroidered silk, unable to sleep for more than an hour due to anxious thoughts about military campaigns and state finances.

Akbar complained to Birbal: 'I possess the softest mattress in the empire, scented with lavender and rosewater, yet sleep eludes me! Yet early this morning, I saw an ordinary sentry sleeping soundly upon the cold, hard marble flagstones, snoring in blissful peace! How can a slab of rock be softer than royal velvet?'

Birbal smiled: 'Sire, sleep does not rest upon feathers or silk; sleep rests upon physical exhaustion and a mind free from guilt and anxiety. If you wish to understand, let us trade places with the sentry tonight.'

Akbar agreed to an experiment. That afternoon, Birbal invited Akbar to spend four hours working disguised as ordinary laborers in the palace stables, carrying heavy bales of hay, shoveling grain, and sweeping the stone yards under the afternoon sun.

By sunset, Akbar's muscles ached, his hands were calloused, and his brow was drenched in sweat.

Birbal led the exhausted Emperor to a simple wooden bench in a garden pavilion, offering him a dry barley chapati and a cup of fresh well water.

Akbar ate the simple bread with ravenous hunger, lay his head down upon the hard wooden bench, and within two minutes, fell into a deep, peaceful, unbroken slumber that lasted until the morning sun kissed his face!

Awakening refreshed and invigorated, Akbar exclaimed: 'Birbal! I have not slept so deeply in twenty years! This wooden bench felt like the gardens of paradise!'

Birbal said with a gentle bow: 'You see, Your Majesty? Sleep cannot be purchased with gold, nor summoned by velvet cushions. Physical labor tires the body, and honest contentment quiets the mind. The poor laborer sleeps on stone because he has worked hard and has no kingdoms to worry over; the monarch tosses on silk because his mind carries the weight of an empire.'

Akbar took the lesson deeply to heart, resolving to balance state duties with simple exercise and a calm spirit.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
